expectedText:
VEXATIOUS LITIGANT DESIGNATION IN FAMILY COURT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Pat Morgan

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's vexatious litigant statute, Code of Civil Procedure sections 391 through 391.7, as it can apply in a family law proceeding between Jordan Lee and Pat Morgan, case number CGC-26-123456, filed in Sacramento County. It covers the statutory definition of a "vexatious litigant," a 2023 addition to that definition specific to a person restrained by a domestic violence restraining order, the motion procedure for requiring security or a prefiling order, and the automatic stay and dismissal consequences that can follow. It does not state whether either party in this matter is or is not a vexatious litigant, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney about the facts of a specific case.

STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "VEXATIOUS LITIGANT"
California law defines a "vexatious litigant" to include a person who, in the immediately preceding seven-year period, has commenced, prosecuted, or maintained in propria persona at least five litigations other than in small claims court that were finally determined adversely to the person or unjustifiably left pending at least two years without trial or hearing; a person who repeatedly relitigates, in propria persona, an already-finally-determined matter against the same defendant; a person who, while acting in propria persona, repeatedly files unmeritorious motions or papers, conducts unnecessary discovery, or engages in other frivolous or delay-only tactics; or a person previously declared a vexatious litigant by any state or federal court of record in an action based on the same or substantially similar facts. "Litigation" for these purposes means any civil action or proceeding commenced, maintained, or pending in any state or federal court.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Vexatious litigant” means a person who does any of the following: (1) In the immediately preceding seven-year period has commenced, prosecuted, or maintained in propria persona at least five litigations other than in a small claims court that have been (i) finally determined adversely to the person or (ii) unjustifiably permitted to remain pending at least two years without having been brought to trial or hearing."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391(a)-(b)(1)-(4) (California Legislative Information text), the statutory definitions of "litigation" and "vexatious litigant," first four categories (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=391.)
  Known gap: This clause states the first four of five statutory definitional categories in Code of Civil Procedure section 391(b); the fifth, domestic-violence-restraining-order-based category added effective January 1, 2023, is covered in a separate clause. The statute's numeric threshold (five qualifying litigations in seven years) and its "finally determined adversely" and "unjustifiably permitted to remain pending" language are not further defined within section 391 itself, and no case law interpreting how family law motions or orders to show cause count toward that threshold could be verified for this clause because CourtListener's case-law search returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, daily quota exhausted) on the single query attempted for this research.

VEXATIOUS LITIGANT STATUS BASED ON VIOLATING A DOMESTIC VIOLENCE RESTRAINING ORDER
A fifth, family-law-specific category was added to the vexatious litigant definition effective January 1, 2023. A person qualifies as a vexatious litigant if, after being restrained by a restraining order issued at a hearing under the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (Family Code section 6300 et seq.), and while that restraining order remains in place, the person commenced, prosecuted, or maintained one or more litigations against the protected person in any court or jurisdiction, where those litigations are determined to be meritless and caused the protected person to be harassed or intimidated.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(5) After being restrained pursuant to a restraining order issued after a hearing pursuant to Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 6300) of Part 4 of Division 10 of the Family Code, and while the restraining order is still in place, they commenced, prosecuted, or maintained one or more litigations against a person protected by the restraining order in this or any other court or jurisdiction that are determined to be meritless and caused the person protected by the order to be harassed or intimidated."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391(b)(5) (California Legislative Information text), the domestic-violence-restraining-order-based vexatious litigant category; not an independent source from the other § 391(b) categories cited in this document's companion clause, as both come from the same statutory section (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=391.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory subdivision, added by a 2022 amendment (AB 2391, effective January 1, 2023), and it is the only subdivision of section 391(b) quoted for this clause; it is not an independent source from the other four categories in section 391(b), all of which appear in the same section and same amendment history. The statute does not itself define "meritless" or "harassed or intimidated" for purposes of this subdivision, and no published case applying this relatively new provision could be verified because of the CourtListener rate-limit failure disclosed elsewhere in this research.

MOTION FOR SECURITY OR DISMISSAL; NO FILING FEE FOR A PROTECTED PERSON'S MOTION
In any pending litigation, at any time until final judgment, a defendant may move the court, on notice and hearing, for an order requiring the plaintiff to furnish security, or for an order dismissing the litigation under the merits-based dismissal provision described elsewhere in this document. A motion for security must be based on, and supported by a showing, that the plaintiff is a vexatious litigant and that there is not a reasonable probability the plaintiff will prevail against the moving defendant. Where the motion is based on the domestic-violence-restraining-order category of the vexatious litigant definition, it may be brought only by the person protected by the restraining order, and that person is not required to pay a filing fee for the motion.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) In any litigation pending in any court of this state, at any time until final judgment is entered, a defendant may move the court, upon notice and hearing, for an order requiring the plaintiff to furnish security or for an order dismissing the litigation pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 391.3. The motion for an order requiring the plaintiff to furnish security shall be based upon the ground, and supported by a showing, that the plaintiff is a vexatious litigant and that there is not a reasonable probability that they will prevail in the litigation against the moving defendant."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391.1(a) (California Legislative Information text), the general motion procedure for security or dismissal (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=391.1.)
  "(b) A motion pursuant to subdivision (a) on the grounds that plaintiff is a vexatious litigant pursuant to paragraph (5) of subdivision (b) of Section 391 may be brought only by a person protected by the restraining order. A person filing a motion as described in this subdivision shall not be required to pay a filing fee."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391.1(b) (California Legislative Information text), the restraining-order-based motion and its filing-fee exemption; from the same statutory section as the citation above, not an independent source (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=391.1.)
  Known gap: This clause combines subdivisions (a) and (b) of the same statutory section (section 391.1); they are not independent sources of one another. The statute does not specify a filing fee exemption for a motion brought on any basis other than the restraining-order-based category, and it does not state whether the fee waiver in subdivision (b) extends to any other papers filed in connection with the same motion.

HEARING ON THE MOTION DOES NOT DECIDE THE MERITS
At the hearing on a motion for security, the court considers any evidence material to the ground of the motion, written or oral, by witnesses or affidavit. Except for an order dismissing the litigation under the merits-based dismissal provision described elsewhere in this document, no determination the court makes in ruling on the motion is, or is deemed to be, a determination of any issue in the underlying litigation or of its merits.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "At the hearing upon the motion the court shall consider any evidence, written or oral, by witnesses or affidavit, as may be material to the ground of the motion. Except for an order dismissing the litigation pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 391.3, no determination made by the court in determining or ruling upon the motion shall be or be deemed to be a determination of any issue in the litigation or of the merits thereof."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391.2 (California Legislative Information text), the hearing procedure and non-merits-determination rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=391.2.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory section describing the evidentiary and non-merits-determination rules for the security motion hearing; it does not describe the evidentiary standard or procedure applicable to a hearing on a prefiling order under the separate statute covering that subject, addressed in another clause of this document.

ORDER REQUIRING SECURITY, OR DISMISSAL FOR MERITLESS FILINGS BY A REPRESENTED-TURNED-SELF-REPRESENTED LITIGANT
If, after hearing the evidence, the court determines the plaintiff is a vexatious litigant and there is no reasonable probability the plaintiff will prevail against the moving defendant, the court orders the plaintiff to furnish security, in an amount and within a time the court fixes, for the moving defendant's benefit. A separate, narrower dismissal remedy applies only where the litigation was filed by a vexatious litigant already subject to a prefiling order, who was represented by counsel when the litigation was filed and became self-represented after that counsel withdrew: if the court determines the litigation has no merit and was filed for purposes of harassment or delay, the court orders it dismissed. A defendant may move for relief under either provision in the alternative but must combine all grounds for relief in one motion.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) Except as provided in subdivision (b), if, after hearing the evidence upon the motion, the court determines that the plaintiff is a vexatious litigant and that there is no reasonable probability that the plaintiff will prevail in the litigation against the moving defendant, the court shall order the plaintiff to furnish, for the benefit of the moving defendant, security in such amount and within such time as the court shall fix."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391.3(a) (California Legislative Information text), the general security order standard (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=391.3.)
  "(b) If, after hearing evidence on the motion, the court determines that the litigation has no merit and has been filed for the purposes of harassment or delay, the court shall order the litigation dismissed. This subdivision shall only apply to litigation filed in a court of this state by a vexatious litigant subject to a prefiling order pursuant to Section 391.7 who was represented by counsel at the time the litigation was filed and who became in propria persona after the withdrawal of his or her attorney."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391.3(b) (California Legislative Information text), the narrower merits-based dismissal remedy; from the same statutory section as the citation above, not an independent source (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=391.3.)
  Known gap: This clause combines subdivisions (a) through (c) of the same statutory section (section 391.3); they are not independent sources of one another. The statute's "no reasonable probability" and "no merit" standards are not further defined within the statute's own text, and no case law construing how courts apply these standards could be verified because of the CourtListener rate-limit failure disclosed elsewhere in this research.

DISMISSAL FOR FAILURE TO FURNISH ORDERED SECURITY
When security that a court has ordered furnished is not furnished as ordered, the litigation is dismissed as to the defendant for whose benefit the security was ordered.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "When security that has been ordered furnished is not furnished as ordered, the litigation shall be dismissed as to the defendant for whose benefit it was ordered furnished."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391.4 (California Legislative Information text), the automatic-dismissal consequence for failing to furnish ordered security (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=391.4.)
  Known gap: This is a single, short statutory section (unchanged since its original 1963 enactment) that does not itself specify a grace period, a procedure for extending the time to furnish security, or what happens to claims against any other defendant not named as the beneficiary of the security order.

AUTOMATIC STAY OF THE LITIGATION WHILE THE SECURITY MOTION IS PENDING
When a motion for security is filed before trial, the litigation is automatically stayed, and the moving defendant need not plead, until 10 days after the motion is denied, or, if granted, until 10 days after the required security has been furnished and the moving defendant given written notice of that fact. If the motion is made later than before trial, the court determines the length of the stay following denial of the motion or furnishing of the required security.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Except as provided in subdivision (b) of Section 391.3, when a motion pursuant to Section 391.1 is filed prior to trial the litigation is stayed, and the moving defendant need not plead, until 10 days after the motion shall have been denied, or if granted, until 10 days after the required security has been furnished and the moving defendant given written notice thereof."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391.6 (California Legislative Information text), the automatic stay triggered by filing a security motion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=391.6.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory section describing the stay that follows the filing of a security motion under section 391.1; it does not by itself describe the separate automatic stay that can arise from a notice filed under the prefiling-order statute, which is addressed in another clause of this document.

PREFILING ORDER AND ITS EXPRESS REACH INTO FAMILY CODE PROCEEDINGS
A court may, on its own motion or a party's motion, enter a prefiling order prohibiting a vexatious litigant from filing any new litigation in California courts while self-represented without first obtaining leave of the presiding justice or presiding judge of the court where the filing is proposed; disobeying the order can be punished as contempt of court. The presiding justice or judge permits the filing only if it appears the litigation has merit and was not filed for harassment or delay, and may condition permission on the furnishing of security. For purposes of the prefiling-order statute specifically, "litigation" is defined to include any petition, application, or motion -- other than a discovery motion -- in a proceeding under the Family Code or Probate Code, for any order. A court clerk may not file a self-represented vexatious litigant's litigation without that leave; if filed by mistake, notice of the prefiling order automatically stays the litigation, which is then automatically dismissed unless the plaintiff obtains leave within 10 days. The clerk of the court must provide the Judicial Council a copy of each prefiling order, and the Judicial Council maintains and annually disseminates a statewide list of persons subject to a prefiling order.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) In addition to any other relief provided in this title, the court may, on its own motion or the motion of any party, enter a prefiling order which prohibits a vexatious litigant from filing any new litigation in the courts of this state in propria persona without first obtaining leave of the presiding justice or presiding judge of the court where the litigation is proposed to be filed. Disobedience of the order by a vexatious litigant may be punished as a contempt of court."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391.7(a) (California Legislative Information text), the prefiling order authority and its contempt enforcement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=391.7.)
  "(d) For purposes of this section, “litigation” includes any petition, application, or motion other than a discovery motion, in a proceeding under the Family Code or Probate Code, for any order."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391.7(d) (California Legislative Information text), the definition of "litigation," for purposes of the prefiling-order statute only, as reaching Family Code and Probate Code filings; from the same statutory section as the citation above, not an independent source (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=391.7.)
  Known gap: This clause combines several subdivisions of the same statutory section (section 391.7); they are not independent sources of one another. The prefiling-order statute's definition of "litigation" as reaching Family Code and Probate Code petitions, applications, and motions (other than discovery motions) applies only for purposes of that section, not for the broader definitional threshold in section 391(b)(1)-(4) described in a companion clause of this document -- the statute does not say whether a family law motion filed against a prefiling-order requirement also counts toward that separate five-litigation threshold. No published California case interpreting this section's application to family law filings specifically could be verified because the single CourtListener query attempted for this research returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, 125/day quota exhausted).

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Jordan Lee and Pat Morgan acknowledge having reviewed this information sheet describing California's vexatious litigant statute, Code of Civil Procedure sections 391 through 391.7, including the general definitional categories, the domestic-violence-restraining-order-based category added in 2023, the motion procedure for security and its filing-fee exemption for a protected person, the automatic stay, the dismissal consequences, and the prefiling-order procedure's express application to Family Code and Probate Code filings. Signed in Oakland, California on September 1, 2026.

Signed in Oakland, California on September 1, 2026.
